results.title: bayesian - What are posterior predictive checks and what makes them useful? - Cross Validated
results.content: # What are posterior predictive checks and what makes them useful? 1. What exactly is the posterior predictive check? 2. Why do some authors say that running posterior predictive checks is "using the data twice" and should not be abused ? Posterior predictive checks are, in simple words, "simulating replicated data under the fitted model and then comparing these to the observed data" (Gelman and Hill, 2007, p. Posterior predictive checks are helpful in assessing if your model gives you "valid" predictions about the reality - do they fit the observed data or not. > Comparing the predictive distribution $y^\text{rep}$ to the observed data $y$ is generally termed a "posterior predictive check". > Posterior predictive checks (via the predictive distribution) involve a double-use of the data, which violates the likelihood principle. However, arguments have been made in favor of posterior predictive checks, provided that usage is limited to measures of discrepancy to study model adequacy, not for model comparison and inference (Meng 1994).

results.title: Posterior Predictive Checks: Practical Steps
results.content: In this tutorial, we take you through a step-by-step practical guide on how to perform posterior predictive checks, starting from fitting your Bayesian model, simulating replicated data, comparing these simulations with your observed data, and finally interpreting diagnostic outputs. Posterior predictive checks are a diagnostic tool used in Bayesian inference to assess how well a model captures the characteristics of observed data. In Bayesian statistics, after obtaining the posterior distribution $$ p(\theta \mid y) $$ of the parameters $$ \theta $$ given the data $$ y $$, one can generate replicated data sets, denoted as $$ y^{\text{rep}} $$, using the model’s likelihood conditioned on parameters drawn from the posterior. Before performing a posterior predictive check, the first requirement is to fit your Bayesian model to the data. ppc = pm.sample_posterior_predictive(trace, model=model) ### Handling Data Structures Depending on your data, the replication process may need extra care: - **Multivariate Data:** For datasets with multiple variables, ensure that your replicated draws maintain the correlations and structure observed in the data. flowchart TD A["Observed Data"] B["Model Fitting"] C["Posterior Samples"] D["Simulated Replicated Data"] E["Graphical Comparison"] A --> B B --> C C --> D A --> E D --> E. PPC p-values provide a measure of whether the observed data is consistent with data generated under the model. data { int N; vector[N] X; vector[N] Y; } parameters { real alpha; real beta; real sigma; } model { Y ~ normal(alpha + beta * X, sigma); // Likelihood // Priors alpha ~ normal(0, 10); beta ~ normal(0, 10); sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5); } generated quantities { vector[N] Y_rep; for (n in 1:N) Y_rep[n] = normal_rng(alpha + beta * X[n], sigma); } In PyMC, the implementation would follow a similar pattern: ```python import pymc3 as pm with pm.Model() as model: # Priors alpha = pm.Normal('alpha', mu=0, sigma=10) beta = pm.Normal('beta', mu=0, sigma=10) sigma = pm.HalfCauchy('sigma', beta=5) # Likelihood mu = alpha + beta * X Y_obs = pm.Normal('Y_obs', mu=mu, sigma=sigma, observed=Y) # Sampling from the posterior trace = pm.sample(2000, tune=1000) # Posterior predictive checks ppc = pm.sample_posterior_predictive(trace) After fitting the models using either Stan or PyMC, the next step is to generate posterior predictions and perform comparisons, as described earlier.

results.title: Exploratory Analysis of Bayesian Models - 5  Prior and Posterior predictive checks
results.content: The idea behind posterior predictive checks is very general and simple: if a model is good it should be able generate data resembling the observed data (Gelman et al. As in posterior predictive checks we use the data twice, first for fitting the model and then for checking it. If we want a numerical summary of a posterior predictive checks using test statistics we can compute the proportion of simulated data that is less than or equal to the observed data: \[ p(T\_{\text{sim}} \le T\_{\text{obs}} \mid \tilde y) \] The intuition is that if the model can generate predictions from the same distribution as the observed data, then the observed data can be thought of as just one random sample from the posterior predictive distribution.

results.content: # using Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) to compare models with different sample size. I'm using k-fold cross-validation to compare different models. Now I fitted n-different models to the training set and calculated the RMSE on both the training and the test sets. From what I understand, the model having the lower RMSE in the test set should be the preferable one. So I find myself comparing a first model with say n NAs with a second one having 10n NAs. In this way I'm comparing models that are fitted to a different number of observations. 1) Is this an issue when comparing RMSE calculated on the test set? I know for example that, if I was comparing models on the training set, the AIC would not be meaningful in this case, less sure for the R-squared... 2) since I run each model 10 times on 10 training sets and tested on 10 test sets (see beginning for explanations), for a given model I have average RMSE and its standard error on both training and test sets.
